Name: diversity_budgeting_neff
Title: N_eff: Error Correlation, Not Sample Count, Governs Parallel Test-Time Compute
Short Hypothesis: The returns from parallel test-time compute (self-consistency, best-of-N) are governed almost entirely by the *error correlation* between samples, not by their number: an effective-sample-size law acc(N; p, rho) predicts where scaling saturates, and reasoning-optimized (RLVR/long-CoT) models have systematically higher rho than their base/instruct counterparts, so they waste parallel compute. Spending a fixed token budget across low-correlation *solution strategies* (representation and answer-preserving problem-space variation) rather than i.i.d. temperature samples should therefore shift the entire compute-accuracy frontier.
Related Work: Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2023) and best-of-N with process/outcome verifiers (Lightman et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024, Generative Verifiers) study *how many* samples and *how to rank* them; compute-optimal scaling work (Snell et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2024 'Large Language Monkeys') characterizes accuracy-vs-N empirically and shows coverage grows while voting saturates. Adaptive-Consistency (Aggarwal et al., 2023) and Certaindex/Dynasor stop sampling early using agreement. Prompt-diversity work (Rephrase-and-Respond, DiVeRSe, multi-agent debate, DOTS, cross-generation reasoning trees) shows varying context helps but does not isolate why. Yue et al. (2025) report RLVR narrows pass@k relative to base models. Our proposal differs on three axes: (i) we introduce a measurable, predictive quantity, per-problem error correlation rho and the resulting effective sample size N_eff = N/(1+(N-1)rho), and show it forecasts saturation points of majority voting and best-of-N across models/datasets, unifying the scattered empirical scaling curves; (ii) we test a mechanistic explanation of the RLVR pass@k collapse as an *error-correlation* increase and check whether it can be undone at test time without retraining; (iii) we turn the analysis into a budget allocation algorithm (diversity budgeting over a portfolio of decorrelated strategies with per-problem routing) that is evaluated at matched token cost, rather than matched N as in prior ensembling papers.
Abstract: Parallel test-time compute -- sampling many chains of thought and aggregating by voting or a verifier -- reliably improves accuracy, but the gains saturate quickly and unpredictably. We argue the controlling variable is not the number of samples N but how correlated their errors are. Treating each sample's error as a Bernoulli variable with marginal error rate 1-p and pairwise correlation rho, standard concentration gives an effective sample size N_eff = N/(1+(N-1)rho), predicting that majority-vote accuracy plateaus at a rho-determined ceiling regardless of budget. We first measure (p, rho) per problem for several open models (Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-7B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct) on GSM8K, MATH-500, AMC/AIME, and GPQA-Diamond, and show that a two-parameter N_eff law forecasts measured maj@N and weighted best-of-N curves and their saturation points with low calibration error. Second, we test the hypothesis that RL/long-CoT reasoning training increases rho: at matched pass@1, reasoning-tuned models exhibit higher error correlation and larger pass@N-minus-maj@N gaps than instruct baselines, explaining why the models built for test-time compute benefit least from parallel sampling. Third, we show rho is an actionable design target: replacing i.i.d. temperature sampling with a *portfolio* of decorrelating operators -- solution-representation variation (natural-language CoT, program-of-thought, backward substitution check, enumeration), and machine-verified answer-preserving problem rewrites -- lowers rho by a large margin and, at matched token cost, dominates self-consistency, adaptive-consistency, and verifier-reranked best-of-N. A cheap two-pilot-sample router further allocates budget across problems. Error correlation gives test-time compute a predictive, controllable axis.
Experiments: (1) Measurement suite: for each of 5 open models (1.5B-8B, served with vLLM) and 4-5 benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH-500, AMC/AIME-24/25, GPQA-Diamond, MMLU-Pro-STEM subset), sample N=64 traces per problem under each diversification operator: (a) temperature/top-p i.i.d. baseline; (b) prompt/persona/instruction paraphrase; (c) representation variation -- NL-CoT, program-of-thought with a Python executor, backward plug-in verification, brute-force enumeration; (d) answer-preserving problem rewrites (variable renaming, fact reordering, unit change, numeric isomorphism) generated by an LLM and *machine-verified* to preserve the gold answer (rejected otherwise); (e) model variation at matched token cost. Estimate per-problem p, pairwise error-agreement rho (intra-class correlation on the error indicator), and empirical N_eff. (2) Predictive test: fit only (p, rho) from a 16-sample calibration subset and predict maj@N and weighted best-of-N for N=2..64 on held-out samples; report mean absolute error on accuracy and on the predicted saturation point N* (where marginal gain < 0.5%). Compare against a naive independent-error model (rho=0) as a baseline. (3) RLVR/long-CoT hypothesis: pair models matched on pass@1 (instruct vs RLVR-distilled; also short-thinking vs long-thinking via budget-forcing on the same reasoning model) and test whether rho and the pass@64 - maj@64 gap increase; test within-model whether truncating thinking length reduces rho. (4) Diversity budgeting algorithm: on a 100-problem calibration split per dataset, greedily select an operator portfolio and mixture weights minimizing predicted error at token budget B (measuring real generated+executed tokens, including cost of rewrite generation); evaluate on the held-out split against self-consistency, Adaptive-Consistency, best-of-N with a generative verifier, and single-long-CoT budget forcing, all at matched total tokens. Metrics: accuracy vs token-budget curves, area under the compute-accuracy curve, and tokens required to match self-consistency's best accuracy. (5) Per-problem routing: draw 2 pilot samples from different operators; use their agreement plus first-100-token entropy to predict rho and route remaining budget across problems (knapsack). Report accuracy at 25%/50% of the uniform budget. (6) Verifier interaction: test whether an off-the-shelf verifier/reward model is miscalibrated across heterogeneous strategies (per-strategy score distributions), and whether simple per-strategy z-normalization restores gains; report accuracy and verifier ranking AUC per strategy.
Risk Factors and Limitations: rho estimates are noisy at N=64, especially for hard problems with p near 0; we mitigate with hierarchical/shrinkage estimation and bootstrap CIs. The N_eff law is an approximation (exchangeability, single dominant wrong answer) and may misfit tasks with heavy-tailed answer distributions; we report where it fails as a finding. Answer-preserving rewrites are only reliably verifiable for tasks with checkable gold answers, limiting coverage on GPQA-style questions; unverified rewrites could inject label noise. Some operators (program-of-thought) are not available or helpful for non-math domains, so portfolio gains may be domain-dependent. Token-cost accounting across operators (code execution, rewrite generation) requires care and could be contested; we report both token and wall-clock budgets. The RLVR-correlation result depends on available checkpoint pairs matched on pass@1, which may confound training data differences; we mitigate with the within-model thinking-length ablation. Finally, gains may shrink for very strong frontier models we cannot afford to sample at scale; we include a limited API-model spot-check.
